Keturah
keh-TOO-ruh
proper noun (person)
Hebrew Qeturah, "incense"; the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death, mother of six sons.

📖 Biblical Definition

Keturah was the wife (also called a concubine) whom Abraham took after the death of Sarah, by whom he had six more sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Gen 25:1-2; 1 Chr 1:32). From these descended various Arabian peoples, most notably the Midianites through Midian. Yet Scripture is careful to mark the distinction of the covenant line: "Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac. But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country" (Gen 25:5-6). The sons of Keturah were blessed with gifts and a place, but the covenant promise and inheritance passed through Isaac, the son of promise, alone. Keturah's many sons fulfilled in part God's word that Abraham would be a father of many nations, even as the line of redemption ran through the one chosen seed. Keturah stands in the dictionary as Abraham's later wife and the mother of many peoples, a witness both to the breadth of God's promise that Abraham should father many nations, and to the particularity of the covenant, which passed not to all his sons but to Isaac, the child of promise, through whom the blessing of all nations would finally come in Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Abraham's wife after Sarah's death (Gen 25:1-2), mother of six sons including Midian; her sons received gifts but the covenant inheritance passed to Isaac alone, marking the particularity of the promise.

KETURAH, proper noun. "Incense"; the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death.

Mother of six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Gen 25:1-2).

Ancestress of Arabian peoples, including the Midianites.

Her sons received gifts and were sent eastward (Gen 25:6).

The covenant inheritance passed to Isaac, the son of promise.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 25:1 — "Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah."

Gen 25:5 — "And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac."

Gen 25:6 — "But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country."

Gen 17:5 — "...for a father of many nations have I made thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Keturah's account honors the recovery of the particularity of the covenant alongside the breadth of God's promise, against a universalism that erases the distinction of the chosen line of redemption.

expand to see more

Covenant-flattened correction. It might seem that all Abraham's sons should share alike in the promise; Scripture marks a clear distinction: Isaac received the inheritance, the others gifts. The dictionary holds the particularity of the covenant: God's redemptive line ran not through every descendant but through the chosen seed, Isaac, and then Jacob, narrowing to the one Seed, Christ. The breadth of God's mercy to the nations does not erase the particular line through which redemption came.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the harmony of God's universal promise and His particular election. Abraham was made "a father of many nations" (Gen 17:5), fulfilled in part through Keturah's many sons; yet the covenant blessing came through Isaac alone. The dictionary commends both truths: God's purpose embraces all nations, and accomplishes it through a particular, chosen line, until in Christ the blessing of Abraham reaches every family of the earth.
